title: Multiplay: Preserving Intent Over Implementation
carouselSummary: Rebuilding the Multiplay customer dashboard while learning a long-lived platform, working from API contracts and adapting as the team uncovered what customers needed.

content.content:
## Project Context

- Multiplay was founded in 1997 and, over its lifetime, passed through Multiplay, Game and Unity.
- At its core, Multiplay is a game server hosting and management platform. It enables game studios to configure, deploy and operate the server infrastructure behind online games.
- Under Unity, customers used two dashboard experiences:
  - **ClanForge** was the established interface for configuring fleets, managing game images and server profiles, and monitoring game servers.
  - **Self-Service Dashboard** offered a more streamlined experience on the same hosting technology, with closer integration into Unity’s other products.

## Introduction

In December 2025, Rocket Science began the process of taking stewardship of Multiplay from Unity, with full ownership beginning in March 2026. As part of this transition, our pod was responsible for rebuilding the Multiplay customer dashboard experience. The frontend pod consisted of a few engineers over the course of the project, but I was the constant throughout, which meant I developed the most complete view of the dashboard work and naturally took on technical ownership of the frontend output.

As is typical of long-lived production products, the existing application had evolved over many years, with domain knowledge accumulating in its codebase. We had to trace that knowledge through the control flow, data transformations, conditional behaviour and edge cases to understand why the dashboards behaved as they did.

## Learning an Established System While Rebuilding It

When we started rebuilding the Multiplay Dashboard, we didn’t have the time to understand every part of the existing system before development began. We were learning the domain, understanding existing behaviour and building the replacement concurrently.

We knew from the beginning that we were going to have to make some pretty broad assumptions and stay flexible enough to adapt if and when those assumptions were challenged. These assumptions shaped early decisions such as:

- Choosing which technology and UI component libraries to use
- Deciding the priority order of what to build
- Migrating multiple existing dashboards into one—yes, I’m looking at you, ClanForge 🔫

As we developed the replacement and tried to understand the legacy application, it was easy to get distracted by rabbit holes of investigation that simply weren’t worth the energy at *that* point in time. To counteract this, we had to put blinkers on and stay focused on a single page, and often a single flow within that page. We’d follow a flow in Multiplay by Unity, inspect the API calls it triggered, and trace the behaviour through the existing codebase until we understood it well enough to build our version.

This required us to be comfortable accumulating technical debt. We were building against our best understanding of the system at that point in time, knowing that something we learnt later could challenge assumptions we’d already made. Trying to account for every possible future discovery would have slowed us down considerably, so sometimes the right decision was to build what we understood today and accept that we might need to revisit it tomorrow. The important part was knowing where we’d made those compromises, rather than pretending the uncertainty didn’t exist.

## Building Against a Contract, Not a System

While we were migrating the frontend of Multiplay, another pod was migrating the backend services. This meant the majority of the dashboard migration was done without a live backend to validate our interpretations. We *had* to trust that what the API contracts said would happen, actually would happen, making educated assumptions about system behaviour wherever we ran into ambiguity.

To solve this on the frontend, we generated typed TypeScript API clients from those specs. This gave us everything we could reasonably expect—types, API paths and HTTP status codes—everything except realistic, valid data. Where possible, we poked Unity’s existing services to see how they behaved and what data they returned, but that wasn’t always an option. Instead, we leaned heavily on [MockServer](https://www.mock-server.com/) (<3) for most of our development. It allowed us to quickly simulate how we *believed* the Multiplay backend services *would* behave, letting us validate page renders, user interaction behaviour and error states on the fly.

But this still left a lot of uncertainty. Questions like these plagued us during development:

- How should a system behave when you kick off an async process, such as spinning up a fleet?
- How long does it actually take to fire off a test allocation?
- What are the log file types we need to support?

Honestly, we simply didn’t know. We assumed, we guessed, but we didn’t know for sure. We added these to the list of things we *knew* we would have to change, intentionally keeping those areas flexible.

There is always a risk in just trusting a contract. There are the “what ifs,” the doubts, and the unknown dragons waiting to be released when you finally connect the frontend to the backend. Aside from just the data connection, there are the inevitable joys of CORS policies, authentication flows, and all the other invisible hurdles that only appear when two systems finally talk.

We knew this risk and called it out early on, so we prepared. When it came time to connect the FE to the BE, we didn’t do it all at once. We tested the connection service by service, fully verifying the implementation through cURL and Postman requests before routing it through the actual dashboard. And after a day of standard teething issues... it just worked. Most of the assumptions we made were just correct, and the ones that weren’t were quickly resolved.

## Preserving Intent, Not Implementation

When rebuilding an established system, the behaviour you see is evidence of what the system has done, but it does not always tell you what the replacement needs to do. Over time, products accumulate features and approaches from earlier versions. We needed to understand which behaviours still served a customer need and which were just a part of the platform’s history, so we could focus on the workflows that still mattered.

One of the clearest examples was that Unity supported legacy and newer API versions for builds and build configurations. We needed to understand why both existed and whether customers still needed the new dashboard to support both. Rebuilding both approaches would have carried the compatibility burden into the new product, making it harder to move customers towards the newer version in the future. We made the case for supporting the newer approach and asking our support team to help customers migrate instead. We also designed a proof of concept for supporting both if we needed it. After launch, customers were migrated over, and the additional compatibility work wasn’t needed.

We didn’t need to preserve Unity’s implementation to keep the functionality customers relied on. Both dashboards needed to show users accurate, up-to-date information, but we changed how that information was fetched and refreshed. We used stale-while-revalidate (SWR) to handle fetching, retries and revalidation, and added our own application-level error handling. This also let us extend the existing experience with functionality such as refresh buttons that could update the relevant data on a page concurrently.

Graphs and metrics were another example. We needed to understand how Unity’s dashboard presented different types of data and what users needed to see from those views. The dashboards use different graphing methods, but the purpose remained the same: helping users understand metrics across their fleets and on individual servers. By focusing on that purpose, we could change how the graphs worked without losing the information they were there to provide.

## Reversible Decisions and Deliberate Rework

It’s okay to change your mind. It’s perfectly fine to look at an implementation you built for one area and decide it *just* isn’t the right approach when building the rest of the application.

Deciding exactly *when* to rework something, however, is a delicate balancing act. Refactoring early can pay massive dividends if it’s a high-cost pattern used consistently, but reworking too early can drain your team’s resources if you end up having to rework the rework. We needed enough certainty before pulling a pattern out to make it generic and reusable. For us, the canary in the coal mine was usually the moment we caught ourselves copy-pasting code. Once we saw the same pattern required a second or third time, it was a signal that the implementation warranted further attention.

Of course, confidence in a refactor depends in part on confidence in your testing. When the test suite accurately validates the behaviour you’re changing, it gives you more confidence to refactor. Tests don’t remove every risk, but they should help you understand when a change has affected something that already worked.

Windows support was one decision we had to reverse. While looking at Unity’s dashboard, we could see that the APIs appeared to support Windows build configurations and fleets, but we couldn’t find corresponding support in the UI code we examined. We assumed Windows fleets had been deprecated and left them out. Later, we learned that assumption was wrong. We had kept the implementation flexible, so adding Windows support was straightforward once we understood it was needed.

Throughout the migration of the Multiplay Dashboard, our code and processes evolved as we learned more. Each new page gave us a chance to try an approach, refine it and improve on what we’d done before. As those approaches developed across the application, we looped back through earlier pages to apply what we’d learned more widely.

### Keeping Our AI Tooling Up to Date

Deliberately reworking a core pattern also meant updating the instructions we gave our AI agents. We used AI throughout the project to help build workflows, apply stale-while-revalidate (SWR) behaviour to API calls, and configure mock servers. We gave our agents project-specific instructions so their output would fit our architecture, but as our code and patterns improved, those instructions needed to change too. Otherwise, we could be trying to introduce a new pattern while our agents kept generating code in a style we had already moved away from.

Ultimately, reversing a technical decision isn’t a sign that the original decision was a mistake. It can simply mean that we learned more about the system, adapted, and found a better way of doing things.

## Moving Forward Without Perfect Information

Migrating a platform with the history and scale of Multiplay was never going to be a clean, linear process. If we had waited for flawless documentation, a fully built backend, and a complete understanding of every historical edge case, we would never have shipped.

Rebuilding an established system means accepting ambiguity and learning to work through it. We used API contracts and mock servers to keep development moving, put blinkers on to avoid legacy rabbit holes, and treated existing behaviour as evidence of intent rather than a specification we had to reproduce.

We accepted short-term technical debt where we needed to, then revisited components and processes as our understanding improved. By focusing on the intent behind the existing product, we were able to deliver a production dashboard within a short delivery window, despite the uncertainty around us. The goal was never to reproduce every behaviour we found. It was to understand what customers needed from it, then build a dashboard that carried those needs forward.
